stories.summary: Washington and Tehran again presented sharply contrasting narratives over the Strait of Hormuz, underscoring skepticism over the reopening of the waterway. Hours after US President Donald Trump said his forces had “total control” over Hormuz , Iranian officials said his remarks “ do not change the reality ” of its closure. The Wall Street Journal said tracking data showed just 14 ships traversed the channel on Tuesday, barely a tenth of pre-war levels , though a leading Bloomberg columnist suggested that analysts were likely underestimating the volume of oil crossing Hormuz: He noted that visible oil spills pointed to a battle between Iran trying to keep the strait closed while others push to keep it open, “ perhaps more successfully than we think .” — Prashant Rao

articles.title: Leadership changes signal Iran expects a long war
articles.author: Prashant Rao
articles.summary: Iran’s recent reshuffle, as well as its shifting battlefield tactics, suggest it is adapting for a lengthening conflict with the US. Tehran has reordered its leadership in part because of repeated assassinations of its top brass by American and Israeli strikes. But recent moves point to how Iran is “ preparing for a prolonged confrontation ,” an expert wrote in Foreign Policy, noting that Iran was centralizing its military apparatus and increasing its focus on offensive operations. The use of a drone swarm against a US fighter jet, meanwhile, pointed to how “Iran has sought to learn and implement important lessons about the modern battlefield ,” in particular from the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the Institute for the Study of War said. — Prashant Rao

stories.summary: Oil prices ticked down despite a lack of progress on peace talks between Washington and Tehran, as the industry’s outlook for global demand weakened and the US showed signs of rebuilding its stocks. The International Energy Agency and OPEC both slashed their demand forecasts, much of which is being driven by the “ ongoing structural decline ” of gasoline vehicles in China as they are replaced by EVs, the IEA said. The IEA also predicted that total oil supply this year would be about 4% lower than in 2025 because of disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. Still, US commercial crude oil inventories, which don’t include the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, posted their largest weekly gain since 2023 as exports and refinery runs ticked down . Meanwhile, environmental watchdogs are warning of a “nightmare scenario” as a huge oil spill begins to hit Oman’s shoreline . — Tim McDonnell

articles.title: US to intensify economic and military pressure on Iran
articles.author: Prashant Rao
articles.summary: Washington signaled it will ramp up economic and military pressure on Tehran, dashing hopes of any imminent respite to the conflict. The US Treasury secretary said he would soon unveil restrictions “ that have never been seen ,” while the country’s defense chief insisted a naval blockade could be maintained “ indefinitely .” Yet signs of strain are apparent: The Wall Street Journal reported that Washington will dispatch an aircraft carrier to relieve one that spent a record number of consecutive days at sea. The White House’s growing focus on economic measures against Iran signals a return to a strategy deployed in the president’s first term, Bloomberg noted, reflecting “ a marked pivot for an administration that has repeatedly threatened a stepped up military campaign.” — Prashant Rao

stories.summary: The US heightened its trade pressure on allies and lashed out at China, raising tensions ahead of a summit of the superpowers’ leaders next month. Washington said Beijing was running a “ Great Transshipment Scam ,” accusing some of its closest partners of enabling China’s efforts to ferry goods via third countries in order to evade US tariffs. The report came as US President Donald Trump unveiled duties of up to 100% on imported drones and drone components, including from a raft of allies. Washington and Beijing also appear to be making no progress towards building a pillar of their trade truce, a bilateral board of investment, the head of a top US business group told the South China Morning Post. — Prashant Rao
